Why Knee Protection Matters

Your knees are among the most exposed joints on a motorcycle. In a slide, the natural tendency is to spread your legs, putting your knees in direct contact with the road surface. The knee joint is complex, fragile, and extremely difficult to repair once damaged. Quality knee armour is not optional for touring — it is essential protection against life-altering injuries.

CE Rating Standards

Knee armour is tested to EN 1621-1 standard:

  • CE Level 1 — Average transmitted force below 35kN. Basic protection suitable for low-speed riding.
  • CE Level 2 — Average transmitted force below 20kN. Significantly better protection and the minimum recommended for touring riders on faster roads.

Armour Materials

Viscoelastic (D3O, SAS-TEC) — Flexible during normal movement but locks rigid on impact. The most comfortable option for long-distance touring as they flex naturally with your knee bend.

Hard shell with foam — Traditional approach using a rigid outer shell over an energy-absorbing foam inner. Proven protection but less flexible and can create pressure points on long rides.

Memory foam — Moulds to your knee shape over time for a custom fit. Good comfort but generally lower protection levels than viscoelastic alternatives.

Positioning Is Everything

The best knee armour in the world is useless if it is not centred over your kneecap. When buying riding trousers or jeans, check the armour sits correctly in both standing and sitting positions. Many trousers offer height-adjustable armour pockets to accommodate different leg proportions. If the armour migrates above or below your knee when riding, it cannot protect the joint effectively.

Best Knee Armour 2026

D3O T5 EVO Pro — The premium CE Level 2 knee protector. Ultra-thin viscoelastic material that flexes freely but absorbs impacts efficiently. Comfortable for all-day touring without pressure points.

SAS-TEC SC-1/06 — Excellent CE Level 2 protector with viscoelastic construction. Slightly thicker than D3O but offers outstanding impact absorption at a lower price.

Forcefield Isolator — Multi-layer CE Level 2 protector with ventilation channels. Flexible and breathable for warm-weather comfort.

Oxford Level 2 Insert — Budget CE Level 2 protector that fits most standard trouser pockets. A worthwhile upgrade from any Level 1 armour.

Always upgrade to CE Level 2 knee armour. The price difference between Level 1 and Level 2 is typically under twenty pounds. The protection difference could save your ability to walk.

Upgrading Factory Armour

Many motorcycle trousers come with basic CE Level 1 knee armour. Upgrading to CE Level 2 is straightforward — simply remove the factory armour from its pocket and insert the upgrade. Most pockets accept standard-sized protectors from D3O, SAS-TEC, or Forcefield. This simple upgrade takes five minutes and significantly improves your knee protection for touring speeds.
keyTakeaways: Knee armour is tested to EN 1621-1, with CE Level 2 transmitting under 20kN versus 35kN for Level 1.
Upgrade to CE Level 2 for touring; the price difference over Level 1 is usually under twenty pounds.
Viscoelastic armour (D3O, SAS-TEC) flexes when riding but locks rigid on impact.
Positioning is critical: armour must stay centred over the kneecap in both standing and sitting positions.
Most factory trouser pockets accept standard upgrade protectors in a five-minute swap.

pros: CE Level 2 nearly halves the impact force reaching your knee.
Viscoelastic armour is flexible and comfortable for all-day touring.
Upgrading factory Level 1 armour is cheap and takes five minutes.
cons: Armour that migrates off the kneecap cannot protect the joint.
Hard-shell types can create pressure points on long rides.
Memory foam moulds well but often offers lower protection levels.

faq.q: What CE level should knee armour be for touring?
faq.a: Knee armour is tested to EN 1621-1. Level 1 transmits an average below 35kN and Level 2 below 20kN, so Level 2 offers significantly better protection. For touring on faster roads, Level 2 is the recommended minimum. The price difference over Level 1 is typically under twenty pounds, which is a very small cost for a meaningful improvement in knee protection.

faq.q: Why does armour positioning matter so much?
faq.a: The best armour in the world is useless if it is not centred over your kneecap. When you buy trousers or jeans, check the armour sits correctly in both standing and sitting positions, because it shifts as you move. Many trousers offer height-adjustable pockets. If the armour rides above or below the joint when you are on the bike, it cannot protect the knee in a slide.

faq.q: Can I upgrade the armour that came with my trousers?
faq.a: Almost always, yes. Many trousers ship with basic Level 1 knee armour. Upgrading is straightforward: remove the factory protector and slide in a Level 2 replacement. Most pockets accept standard-sized protectors from D3O, SAS-TEC or Forcefield. The whole job takes about five minutes and noticeably improves your protection for touring speeds.

faq.q: Which armour material is most comfortable?
faq.a: Viscoelastic materials like D3O and SAS-TEC are the most comfortable for long-distance touring because they stay soft and flex with your knee during normal movement, then stiffen instantly on impact. Hard-shell-and-foam armour is proven but less flexible and can create pressure points, while memory foam is comfortable but generally offers lower protection levels.

faq.q: Do I need knee armour if I wear riding jeans?
faq.a: Yes. Denim, even single-layer aramid denim, protects against abrasion but does little against impact. Knee armour absorbs the shock of hitting the road or an obstacle. Most quality riding jeans include pockets for knee protectors, so fit at least Level 1 and ideally upgrade to Level 2 for the best protection over the complex, fragile knee joint.
